questions.prompt: You estimate the coin lands heads 60% of the time and stake the Kelly fraction of 20%. The true chance is 55%. What happens to your money?
options: It grows at the best possible rate for the true coin
It grows, but at 75% of the best rate
It shrinks slowly, because 20% is twice the true Kelly stake of 10%
It is lost on the first tail
questions.explanation: The true Kelly stake is 0.55 − 0.45 = 0.1. A 20% stake is twice that, and at the true chance it grows at −0.00014 per round, a slow loss.

questions.prompt: With an exact edge, how much of the best growth does half Kelly keep, using 2c − c²?
questions.explanation: With c = 0.5, 2 × 0.5 − 0.5² = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. You keep 75% of the growth while the swings are about half as large.

questions.prompt: In 10,000 simulated 5-year backtests of a strategy whose true Kelly fraction is 1.25, 30% of the estimates were above 2.5. Why does this argue for a fraction of Kelly?
options: Because staking more than twice the true Kelly fraction gives zero growth or a loss, while staking less only grows more slowly
Because a Kelly fraction above 1 is always a mistake in the formula
Because 5 years of data always overstate the edge
Because half of an estimate is always the true value
questions.explanation: The two errors cost different amounts. Too large a stake can stop growth entirely, so cutting the estimate protects you when it is too high, at the price of a little growth when it is right.
